background.definition: Asbestosis is asbestos-induced pulmonary parenchymal fibrosis, with or without pleural thickening.

list.listitem: An estimated 1.3 million people have been exposed to asbestos in the United States.
The incidence of asbestosis is 4 per 10,000 persons in the United States.
Asbestos exposure in high concentrations are associated with cancers of the lung, pleura, gastrointestinal tract, kidney, pancreas, ovary, prostate, and larynx.
Systemic autoimmune disease, particularly rheumatoid arthritis, appears to be a higher-than-expected risk among asbestos-exposed populations.

Asbestos, both the serpentine and amphibole varieties, is used in industry because of its natural properties of flexibility, durability, and resistance to heat and/or chemical corrosion. The principal routes of exposure are (1) mining and milling of fibers, (2) industrial applications of asbestos (textiles, cement, friction materials, insulation, shipbuilding, brakelining mechanics, laggers, pipe cutters), and (3) nonoccupational exposure to airborne asbestos.

Although the United States began asbestos exposure restrictions in 1971, much of the world still widely employs it industrially. In the United States, the current permissible exposure limit is 0.1 fibers/cc for an 8-hour time-weighted average.
Inhaled fibers 0.5 to 5.0 µm are deposited at the bifurcations of alveolar ducts, where they are partially cleared by the mucociliary escalator or transported into the interstitium.
The alveolar ducts and peribronchial regions adjacent to the terminal bronchioles become thickened by interstitial macrophages and fibroblasts.
Alveolar epithelial cells are damaged by both the fibers and the mediators released by macrophages after phagocytosis of free asbestos fibers.
As fibrosis progresses, the lung becomes smaller with diminished capacity for gas exchange.
Consider screening workers exposed to asbestos using chest x-ray and pulmonary function testing (PFT) every 3 to 5 years. C
A high index of suspicion should exist for symptoms or signs of lung cancer, mesothelioma, ovarian, and gastrointestinal cancers (not just colon). C
Among adults with asbestos exposure, do not recommend vitamin A supplementation as it increases lung cancer incidence and mortality as well as all-cause mortality. A
Consider influenza and pneumococcal immunizations for patients with respiratory conditions secondary to asbestosis. C
Use of personal protective equipment (PPE ) such as masks and respirators appears effective in preventing asbestos exposure in workers. B
Asbestosis presents with gradual worsening dyspnea on exertion. C
Clinically, patients with asbestosis have end-inspiratory basilar rales that persist after coughing. C
The chest x-ray findings of small, irregular opacities in the mid- and lower lung fields are classified for quantity, location, and intensity of perfusion by a NIOSH-certified "B-reader." C

Differential.Differential_Features: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis lacks asbestos bodies and has an acinar pattern of fibrosis
Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) reveals a marked lymphocytic alveolitis and the chest radiograph rarely notes pleural thickening or effusion
Asbestos-related emphysema may result in a decreased forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1)/forced vital capacity (FVC) ratio with a reduced FEV1
"Asbestomas" usually occur in background of irregular opacities, and typically require biopsy
Sarcoidosis features hilar/paratracheal lymphadenopathy or evidence of multisystem disease

list.listitem: The most prominent symptom of asbestosis is dyspnea on exertion after a 15- to 20-year latency, which slowly worsens.
Additional symptoms include a cough that can be either dry or productive of clear sputum, and chest pain that may be pleuritic or aching.
Physical examination reveals end-inspiratory basilar rales (32%-64%) that persist after coughing. With extensive disease, clubbing of the fingers (32%-42%) and cor pulmonale may develop.

The diagnosis of asbestosis requires: (1) structural pathology consistent with asbestos-related disease documented by imaging or histology, (2) a reliable history of occupational or environmental asbestos exposure with markers of exposure such as pleural plaques or asbestos bodies, and (3) no other cause of parenchymal lung disease.

The chest x-ray reveals small, irregular opacities in the mid- and lower lung fields. Using a classification system for pneumoconioses "B-readers," grade the opacities and pleural changes by quantity, by location, and intensity of their profusion. The presence of pleural plaques on the parietal pleura is pathognomonic of asbestos exposure.
When using International Labour Organization standards digital radiography is not statistically different from analog film in classifying pneumoconiotic pleural abnormalities.

High-resolution CT (HRCT) imaging is more sensitive and specific than radiography for evaluation of asbestosis. Early in the disease process it can detect subpleural dotlike opacities and branching structures. At 7-10 days following exposure it can identify the presence of benign pleural effusions. HRCT scanning in asbestosis reveals subpleural linear densities (2-5 cm), parenchymal bands, thickened interlobular septa, and honeycombing.

Pulmonary function tests classically reveal a restrictive impairment with decreased FVC, decreased total lung volume, and a diminished carbon monoxide diffusing capacity. Mixed restrictive/obstructive patterns are frequently seen. Hypoxemia may occur at rest or develop with exercise.
The presence of restriction on spirometry is strongly associated with parenchymal abnormalities (OR 2.9; 95% CI 1.4-6.0) and diffuse pleural thickening (OR 4.1; 95% CI 2.1-7.8).

The most definitive evidence is the presence of 1 to 2 asbestos bodies (coated or uncoated asbestos fibers)/cm2 in sputum or BAL. BAL can identify and quantify asbestos bodies and fibers, as they appear to correlate with the presence or degree of interstitial pulmonary fibrosis. The presence of neutrophilia correlates with disturbances in oxygenation. This test is superior to transbronchial biopsy in making the diagnosis.
Suspect asbestosis in a patient presenting with progressive exertional dyspnea beginning 15 to 20 years after asbestos exposure.
Obtain a chest x-ray read by a "B-reader" and PFT as initial studies. A CXR compatible with asbestosis or a restrictive pattern on PFT strongly suggests the diagnosis.
If a mixed or obstructive pattern is seen on PFT, or if the CXR is not comparable with asbestosis, order an HRCT scan and either sputum analysis or bronchoalveolar lavage.
Detection of asbestos bodies or fibers in sputum confirms the diagnosis.
As there is no effective treatment for parenchymal asbestosis, treat the specific diseases and complications resulting from exposure. C
No prophylactic medication or treatment prevents the development or progression of asbestosis or asbestos-related diseases once exposure has occurred.
Effective management of concurrent chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or asthma, if present, may reduce morbidity.
Antibiotics are recommended for suspected bacterial respiratory infections, and diuretics if cor pulmonale develops.

Bevacizumab in combination with pemetrexed disodium plus cisplatin with folic acid and vitamin B12 supplementation increases the median length of survival (18.8 months vs. 16.1 months) compared to pemetrexed disodium plus cisplatin.
Remove patient from further exposure to asbestos, recommend a high-calorie, high-protein diet with advanced disease, and consider a graded exercise program.
Obtain an assessment of functional impairment and rate in accordance with American Thoracic Society criteria.
Recommend pneumococcal pneumonia vaccination and annual influenza immunization.
If the patient smokes, smoking cessation lowers the risk for asbestos-related malignancies.
A Cochrane review found considerable uncertainty for the effectiveness of exercise therapy to improve exercise capacity and quality of life among adults with asbestosis.

Overall prognosis is determined by the total asbestos burden in the lungs, the presence of comorbid conditions, and whether a complication of asbestos-related disease develops. B Dyspnea at rest occurs in 5% of asbestosis patients. B

Patients exposed to asbestos have an increased risk of lung cancer (RR 3.5; 95% CI, 1.7-7.2). B Criteria for LDCT screening for lung cancer in these persons have been suggested but not widely implemented. C
Mesothelioma is uniformly fatal with a median survival of 6 to 18 months. B
Meta-analyses have indicated an increased risk of ovarian cancer (RRs 1.29-1.77). B
